questions.solution: B is on Thursday, so the C–E pair is Mon–Tue, Tue–Wed or Fri–Sat, and D can't be on Wed or Fri. questions.question: With 20 coins, how many coins must Asha remove on her first turn to be sure of winning?
questions.solution: Work backwards: a pile is 'losing' for the player to move if every move leads to a winning pile. 0 is losing. 1, 2 and 4 can reach 0, so they're winning. 3 → 2 or 1 only, so it's losing. In general, the losing piles are exactly the multiples of 3, because 1, 2 and 4 are never multiples of 3. 20 − 2 = 18 is a multiple of 3. Taking 1 (19) or 4 (16) leaves a winning pile for Bilal.

questions.question: For how many starting pile sizes from 1 to 30 (inclusive) can Bilal force a win?
questions.solution: Work backwards: a pile is 'losing' for the player to move if every move leads to a winning pile. 0 is losing. 1, 2 and 4 can reach 0, so they're winning. 3 → 2 or 1 only, so it's losing. In general, the losing piles are exactly the multiples of 3, because 1, 2 and 4 are never multiples of 3. Bilal wins exactly when the start is a multiple of 3: 3, 6, …, 30, which is 10 sizes.

questions.question: Under the standard rule, what is the smallest starting pile larger than 20 with which Bilal can force a win?
questions.solution: Work backwards: a pile is 'losing' for the player to move if every move leads to a winning pile. 0 is losing. 1, 2 and 4 can reach 0, so they're winning. 3 → 2 or 1 only, so it's losing. In general, the losing piles are exactly the multiples of 3, because 1, 2 and 4 are never multiples of 3. The next multiple of 3 after 20 is 21.

questions.question: Suppose players may remove 1, 2, 3 or 4 coins (last coin still wins). With 23 coins, how many should Asha remove first to be sure of winning?
questions.solution: With moves 1–4, the losing piles are multiples of 5 (any move from 5k can be answered to return to 5(k − 1)). Asha should leave 20, so she takes 3.

questions.question: Now suppose the rule is reversed: the player who takes the last coin LOSES (moves are still 1, 2 or 4). With 10 coins, how many should Asha remove first to be sure of winning?
questions.solution: Now a pile of 1 is losing for the player to move, because they must take the last coin. Working upward: 2, 3 → can leave 1, so winning. 4 → leaves 3, 2 or 0, and 0 means you just took the last coin and lost, so 4 is losing. The losing piles are 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, … (one more than a multiple of 3). 10 is losing: from 10, Asha can leave 9, 8 or 6, and each lets Bilal move back to 7. So she cannot force a win.

questions.question: How many students belong to all three clubs?
questions.solution: 48 students are in at least one club. Adding the three club sizes counts students in one club once, in two clubs twice and in all three thrice: 22 + 22 + 25 = 69 = (only one) + 2 × 15 + 3 × (all three). Also (only one) + 15 + (all three) = 48. Subtracting, 69 − 48 = 15 + 2 × (all three), so 3 students are in all three clubs and 30 are in exactly one. So: only Music 10, only Drama 8, only Sports 12, Music & Drama only 5, Music & Sports only 4, Drama & Sports only 6, all three 3, none 12.

questions.question: Who is the thief?
questions.solution: Exactly two people (the thief and the joker) lie. Suppose D tells the truth: then E is the joker, so E's statements are false and B is the thief. But then C, who is neither, must be truthful, and C says the thief is D or E — a contradiction. So D lies. If D were the joker, D's 'I am not the thief' would be false, making D the thief as well — impossible. So D is the thief. Then B's 'C is the thief' is false, so B is the other liar, the joker; B's 'I am not the joker' is indeed false ✓. Check the truth-tellers A, C, E: A is not the thief ✓, C is not the joker ✓; the thief is D ✓, A is not the joker ✓; B is not the thief ✓, D is not the joker ✓. D's 'E is the joker' is false ✓. Checking all 20 thief–joker pairs confirms D is the thief and B the joker, and nothing else works.

questions.question: How many of the six are knights?
questions.solution: Split on B. If B is a knave, A's 'B is a knave' is true, so A is a knight, and C's statement is true (A is a knight), so C is a knight. If E were a knight, D would match A (a knight), D's 'E and F same type' would make F a knight, and F's 'C or E is a knave' would be false — impossible. So E is a knave, D differs from A (a knave), D's lie means F differs from E (F a knight), and F's 'E is a knave' is true ✓. That gives exactly three knights (A, C, F), which makes B's claim true — but B was assumed a knave. So B is a knight. Then A is a knave. If E were a knave, D would differ from A (a knight), so E and F match (F a knave), and F's lie would need both C and E to be knights — but E is a knave. So E is a knight, D is a knave (same as A), D's lie means F differs from E (F a knave), and F's lie means C and E are both knights; C's 'D is a knave or A is a knight' is true ✓. Result: B, C and E are knights; A, D and F are knaves (three knights, so B told the truth ✓). A computer check of all 64 possible assignments confirms this is the only consistent one. So there are 3 knights.

questions.question: What number did S write in round 2?
questions.solution: Count scoring turns. R's 5 must come from two different numbers (1 + 4 or 2 + 3), so R scores in exactly two rounds; P, Q and S each score at least once. That is at least 5 scoring turns. A round with a repeated number has at most 2 scorers, and round 2 has exactly 1, so there are at most 2 + 1 + 2 = 5. Hence exactly 5: P scores once (4, in round 3), Q once (1), S once (2), R twice, and rounds 1 and 3 have two scorers each. Q wrote 4 in round 1 but scored only 1 overall, so Q did not score in round 1; P scored only in round 3. So the round-1 scorers are R and S, and Q's 4 was matched by P: round 1 is P 4, Q 4, S 2, R a with a = 1 or 3. If R scored again in round 3 (and Q in round 2), the totals of the numbers come out to 32 + 2b for a whole number b, never 33 — impossible. So Q scored 1 in round 3 and R scored alone in round 2 with 5 − a. If a = 3, R's numbers 3, 2 and his round-3 number (which must pair with S, avoiding 4 and 1) clash; so a = 1 and R wrote 4 in round 2. Round 2: P, Q, S wrote the same d; round 3: P 4, Q 1, R and S both c (c = 2 or 3). Sum: 11 + (3d + 4) + (5 + 2c) = 33 gives 3d + 2c = 13, so c = 2 and d = 3. Final: round 1 — P 4, Q 4, R 1, S 2; round 2 — P 3, Q 3, R 4, S 3; round 3 — P 4, Q 1, R 2, S 2. A computer check of all 4¹² possibilities confirms it is the only one.

questions.question: How many coins did A hold at the start?
questions.solution: The total, 160 coins, never changes. Work backwards from the end: in the round a player loses, every other player's holding is halved (undoing the doubling) and the loser gets back what he paid. Undoing the rounds for each of the 24 possible orders of losers shows that the round-1 loser always starts with 81 to 84 coins and everyone else with at most 44, so 'B held more than the other three together' means B lost round 1. Of the six orders with B first, only (B, D, A, C) and (B, A, D, C) leave C with the fewest coins at the start, and 'D before A' picks the first. Undoing the rounds for B, D, A, C gives starting holdings A 21, B 82, C 13, D 44. Forward check: after round 1 (B loses) 42, 4, 26, 88; after round 2 (D loses) 84, 8, 52, 16; after round 3 (A loses) 8, 16, 104, 32; after round 4 (C loses) 16, 32, 48, 64 ✓.

questions.question: How many bananas did X get?
questions.solution: Z's six fruits are apples plus equal numbers of oranges and bananas, so Z's apples = 6 − 2 × (Z's bananas), an even number. If Z had 2 or more apples, X would need at least 3 and Y at least 4, which is 9 or more apples, but there are only 7. So Z has 0 apples, 3 bananas and 3 oranges. X has no oranges, so the remaining 5 − 3 = 2 oranges are Y's. Y's other 4 fruits are apples and bananas, and X's 6 fruits are apples and bananas. X and Y share all 7 apples with Y having more: the splits (3, 4), (2, 5) and (1, 6) are possible in principle, but Y can hold at most 4 apples, so X has 3 apples and Y has 4. Then X has 6 − 3 = 3 bananas and Y has 0 bananas. Result: X 3 apples, 3 bananas, 0 oranges; Y 4 apples, 0 bananas, 2 oranges; Z 0 apples, 3 bananas, 3 oranges. A computer check of every possible split confirms this is the only one. X got 3 bananas.

questions.question: What is the total weight (in kg) of all five parcels?
questions.solution: Each parcel appears in 4 of the 10 pairs, so the readings add up to 4 × (total weight): 196 = 4 × total, total = 49 kg. questions.question: How many rounds did Ravi win?
questions.solution: Write RP for 'Ravi rock, Sima paper' and so on; with no draws there are six kinds of round. Let RP = x. Ravi's rocks: RP + RS = 4, so RS = 4 − x. Sima's paper: RP + SP = 3, so SP = 3 − x. Ravi's scissors: SR + SP = 2, so SR = x − 1. Sima's rock: PR + SR = 2, so PR = 3 − x. Ravi's paper: PR + PS = 3, so PS = x. (Sima's scissors: RS + PS = 4 ✓.) questions.question: With as many workers as needed, what is the minimum number of days to finish the whole renovation?
questions.solution: With enough workers, every task starts as soon as its predecessors finish. Finish days: A 3, B 4, C 5, D 9 (after A and B), E 8, F 13 (after D at 9 and E at 8), G 6, H 11. So the project needs 13 days, along the chain B → D → F (4 + 5 + 4). Working backwards from day 13, the latest finishes are A 4, B 4, C 6, D 9, E 9, F 13, G 8, H 13, so the slacks are A 1, B 0, C 1, D 0, E 1, F 0, G 2, H 2.

questions.question: If only two workers are available, what is the minimum number of days needed?
questions.solution: With enough workers, every task starts as soon as its predecessors finish. Finish days: A 3, B 4, C 5, D 9 (after A and B), E 8, F 13 (after D at 9 and E at 8), G 6, H 11. Working backwards from day 13, the latest finishes are A 4, B 4, C 6, D 9, E 9, F 13, G 8, H 13, so the slacks are A 1, B 0, C 1, D 0, E 1, F 0, G 2, H 2. The tasks total 3 + 4 + 2 + 5 + 3 + 4 + 2 + 5 = 28 worker-days, so two workers need at least 14 days. 14 is achievable: worker 1 does A (0–3), C (3–5), D (5–10), F (10–14); worker 2 does B (0–4), G (4–6), E (6–9), H (9–14). Every task starts after its predecessors finish, so the answer is 14.

questions.question: What is the smallest number of workers with which the renovation can still be finished in the minimum possible time found with unlimited workers?
questions.solution: With enough workers, every task starts as soon as its predecessors finish. Finish days: A 3, B 4, C 5, D 9 (after A and B), E 8, F 13 (after D at 9 and E at 8), G 6, H 11. So the project needs 13 days, along the chain B → D → F (4 + 5 + 4). Two workers need at least 28/2 = 14 days, so 13 days needs at least 3. With three it works: start every task as early as possible — at most three tasks (C, D and G, during day 4 to 5) are ever in progress together, so 3 workers suffice.

Step 16: “The stallholder from Nalanda is somewhere to the left of Madhav.” Now fixed: Madhav in stall 2; Nupur in stall 3; Oshin in stall 1; Pankaj in stall 6; Radhika in stall 5; Shaurya in stall 4; Madhav: baskets; Nupur: carpets; Oshin: puppets; Pankaj: bangles; Radhika: masks; Shaurya: dolls; Madhav: 1st; Nupur: 5th; Oshin: 13th; Radhika: 21st; Madhav: Madhubani; Nupur: Kangra; Oshin: Nalanda; Pankaj: Sivasagar; Radhika: Kutch; Shaurya: Bastar. Step 17: “The dolls seller is somewhere to the left of the stall booked on the 3rd.” Now fixed: Pankaj: 3rd; Shaurya: 8th. Every possible arrangement was checked by computer and exactly one fits all the clues: stall 1: Oshin (puppets, 13th, Nalanda); stall 2: Madhav (baskets, 1st, Madhubani); stall 3: Nupur (carpets, 5th, Kangra); stall 4: Shaurya (dolls, 8th, Bastar); stall 5: Radhika (masks, 21st, Kutch); stall 6: Pankaj (bangles, 3rd, Sivasagar). Madhav is Madhav, in stall 2.

b12-clubs.title: Three clubs (Medium)
b12-clubs.html:
Three clubs

A class of 60 students has three clubs: Music, Drama and Sports. A student may join any number of the clubs, including none.

  • Music has 22 members, Drama has 22 and Sports has 25.
  • Exactly 15 students belong to exactly two clubs.
  • 12 students belong to no club.
  • The number of students who are only in Sports is 2 more than the number who are only in Music.
  • Exactly 4 students are in Music and Sports but not in Drama.

b12-countout.title: Counting-out game (Medium)
b12-countout.html:
Counting-out game

Seven children — Anu, Bala, Chetan, Dev, Esha, Farah and Gopal — stand in a circle in that order, clockwise (Gopal is next to Anu). They choose a whole number m from 2 to 9. Starting with Anu as 1, they count clockwise round the circle, and the child who is counted m leaves. Counting starts again at 1 from the next child still in the circle, and so on, until one child is left.

  • Anu was not the first child to leave.
  • Gopal was not among the first three children to leave.
  • Dev was still in the circle when Anu left.

b12-interviews.title: Interview schedule (Medium)
b12-interviews.html:
Interview schedule

Six candidates, P, Q, R, S, T and U, are interviewed one at a time over three days, Monday to Wednesday, with one interview each morning and one each afternoon. Three interviewers, X, Y and Z, each conduct exactly two of the six interviews, and no interviewer conducts two interviews on the same day.

  • X conducts the Monday-morning interview.
  • R is interviewed in an afternoon, by Y.
  • S and T are interviewed on the same day; T is interviewed by Z, and S in the morning.
  • P is interviewed on an earlier day than Q, and both are interviewed by the same interviewer.
  • U is interviewed on Wednesday morning.
  • Z does not conduct any interview on Monday.

b12-knockout.title: Knockout badminton (Medium)
b12-knockout.html:
Knockout badminton

Eight players, A to H, played a knockout badminton tournament. In the quarter-finals A played B, C played D, E played F and G played H. The winner of A–B met the winner of C–D in one semi-final, the winner of E–F met the winner of G–H in the other, and the two semi-final winners met in the final. Every match was the best of three games: the first player to win two games won the match, so each match ended 2–0 or 2–1. There were no walkovers.

  • C did not win a single game in the tournament.
  • D won 5 games in all.
  • B, F and G won exactly one game each.
  • A won 3 games in all.
  • Exactly five matches went to three games.
  • H won fewer games than A.

b12-pipes.html:
Water pipeline network

Water enters a network at junction S at 1,200 litres per minute and flows only along the pipes listed below, in the direction shown. At a junction, all the water that comes in leaves through its outgoing pipes; nothing is stored or lost. The water ends up in three tanks, C, D and E.

b12-rows.title: Two facing rows (Easy)
b12-rows.html:
Two facing rows

Six friends — Amit, Bhavna, Charu, Deepak, Ela and Firoz — sit in two rows of three seats. The north row faces south and the south row faces north, so each person directly faces one person in the other row.

  • Amit sits in the north row, in an end seat, and faces Ela.

  • Bhavna does not face Firoz.

b12-thief.title: The thief and the joker (Medium)
b12-thief.html:
The thief and the joker

Five people, A, B, C, D and E, are questioned about a theft. Exactly one of them is the thief and exactly one other is a joker. The thief and the joker both make two false statements; each of the other three makes two true statements.

  • A: “I am not the thief.” “C is not the joker.”
  • B: “C is the thief.” “I am not the joker.”
  • C: “The thief is D or E.” “A is not the joker.”
  • D: “I am not the thief.” “E is the joker.”
  • E: “B is not the thief.” “D is not the joker.”

b12-vote.title: Preferential vote (Hard)
b12-vote.html:
Preferential vote

120 members elect a president from four candidates, P, Q, R and S. Each member ranks all four candidates. The table shows how many members chose each ranking (first preference on the left); two counts, x and y, are missing.

b2-doubling.title: The doubling game (Hard)
b2-doubling.html:
The doubling game

Four players, A, B, C and D, play four rounds of a game with coins. Each round has exactly one loser, and every player loses exactly one round. The loser of a round pays each of the other three players as many coins as that player holds at that moment, so each of the other three doubles their holding. The loser always has enough coins to pay. No other coins change hands.

  • After the four rounds, A, B, C and D hold 16, 32, 48 and 64 coins respectively.
  • At the start, B held more coins than the other three put together.
  • At the start, C held fewer coins than each of the others.
  • D lost a round before A did.

b2-floors.title: Floors, pets and jobs (Medium)
b2-floors.html:
Floors, pets and jobs

Arjun, Bina, Chetan, Divya and Esha live on floors 1 to 5 of a building (floor 1 is the lowest), one person per floor. Each has a different pet — cat, dog, parrot, fish, rabbit — and a different job — doctor, lawyer, teacher, engineer, pilot.

  • The pilot lives above the dog owner, and the dog owner lives on the floor immediately above the teacher.
  • Arjun lives on the floor immediately below the rabbit owner.
  • The doctor lives on an odd-numbered floor and owns neither the cat nor the dog.
  • Bina lives on an even-numbered floor and is neither the teacher nor the pilot.
  • The fish owner lives exactly three floors below the dog owner.
  • The lawyer owns the cat.
  • Esha lives above Divya but below Bina.

b2-fruit.title: Sharing fruit (Easy)
b2-fruit.html:
Sharing fruit

Seven apples, six bananas and five oranges (18 fruits in all) are shared among three friends, X, Y and Z, so that each friend gets exactly six fruits. It is also known that:

  • X got no oranges.
  • Y got more apples than X, and X got more apples than Z.
  • Z got as many oranges as bananas.

b2-knights.title: Knights and knaves (Hard)
b2-knights.html:
Knights and knaves

On an island every inhabitant is either a knight, who always tells the truth, or a knave, who always lies. Six inhabitants, A, B, C, D, E and F, make one statement each:

  • A: “B is a knave.”
  • B: “Exactly three of us six are knights.”
  • C: “D is a knave, or A is a knight.”
  • D: “E and F are of the same type.”
  • E: “A and D are of the same type.”
  • F: “C is a knave, or E is a knave.”

(“X or Y” is true when at least one of X, Y is true.)

b2-unique.title: The unique-number game (Hard)
b2-unique.html:
The unique-number game

Four players, P, Q, R and S, play three rounds of a game. In each round every player secretly writes a whole number from 1 to 4; different players may write the same number. When the numbers are revealed, a player scores the number he wrote if nobody else wrote that number in that round; otherwise he scores 0 for the round.

  • P scored in round 3.
  • R wrote a different number in each round.
  • At the end of the three rounds, the total scores were P 4, Q 1, R 5 and S 2.
  • The twelve numbers written add up to 33.

  • Either Lalita sits in seat 3 or Nakul sits in seat 1, but not both.
  • Lalita paid by wallet.
  • Ruchi sits to the immediate left of the person who paid by cheque.
  • The person who paid by UPI is also the person who ordered rasmalai.

z1-d19.title: Lecture week (Hard)
z1-d19.html:
Lecture week

Six lectures by Prof. Sen, Prof. Rao, Prof. Pillai, Prof. Mehta, Prof. Khan and Prof. Bose are held on six consecutive days, Monday to Saturday, one per day. Each lecture is in a different hall, Hall A, Hall B, Hall C, Hall D, Hall E and Hall F, and each covers a different topic, comets, fungi, glaciers, monsoons, volcanoes and tides.

The following is known:

  • Prof. Pillai lectures on monsoons.
  • Either the lecturer on tides is scheduled on Wednesday or the lecture in Hall D is scheduled on Tuesday, but not both.
  • There are exactly 4 days between the days of the lecturer on volcanoes and the lecturer on fungi.
  • Prof. Rao lectures on tides.
  • The lecturer on tides and the lecture in Hall C are scheduled on consecutive days.
  • The lecture in Hall D is scheduled on the day immediately before the lecture in Hall A.
  • Prof. Sen and the lecture in Hall F are scheduled on consecutive days.
  • Either Prof. Sen is scheduled on Monday or the lecturer on tides is scheduled on Saturday, but not both.
  • The lecture in Hall B is scheduled on the day immediately before the lecturer on glaciers.
  • The lecture in Hall E is scheduled on either the first or the last day.
  • Prof. Bose is scheduled on some day before the lecturer on monsoons.
  • There are exactly 3 days between the days of Prof. Mehta and the lecturer on volcanoes.

z1-d20.title: Race result (Hard)
z1-d20.html:
Race result

Six cyclists, Ajay, Bhavna, Chirag, Dolly, Ehsan and Farida, finished a race in positions 1 to 6 with no ties (position 1 is the winner, and someone 'ahead of' another finished in a smaller position number). Each rode a bicycle of a different colour, red, blue, green, yellow, white and black; each represented a different club, Falcons, Hawks, Kites, Eagles, Swifts and Herons; and each is a different age, 19, 21, 23, 25, 27 and 29.

The following is known:

  • There are exactly 2 people between Chirag and the rider on the blue bike.
  • The Kites club rider is at one of the two ends.
  • The 19-year-old and Dolly are next to each other.
  • The rider on the white bike and the rider on the red bike are next to each other.
  • The 19-year-old is somewhere ahead of the Herons club rider.
  • Either Ehsan is in position 4 or Bhavna is in position 5, but not both.
  • The rider on the yellow bike is immediately ahead of Dolly.
  • There is exactly one person between Ehsan and Chirag.
  • The 27-year-old is somewhere ahead of Chirag.
  • The rider on the red bike is also the Swifts club rider.
  • Dolly is 25.
  • The Eagles club rider is immediately ahead of Farida.
  • Bhavna is somewhere ahead of the 29-year-old.
  • The rider on the black bike is at one of the two ends.
  • Ajay is at one of the two ends.
  • There is exactly one person between Bhavna and the Falcons club rider.
  • The 29-year-old is somewhere ahead of the Hawks club rider.
  • Farida is 21.

z1-d21.title: Concert order (Hard)
z1-d21.html:
Concert order

Six singers, Gulzar, Harpreet, Indu, Jagan, Komal and Lakshmi, perform one after another in slots 1 to 6 at a concert (slot 1 is first). Each sings in a different language, Tamil, Bangla, Marathi, Telugu, Kannada and Urdu, and each is accompanied by a different instrument, harmonium, sarod, santoor, mridangam, shehnai and guitar.

The following is known:

  • Harpreet and the Bangla singer are next to each other.
  • Either Lakshmi is in slot 1 or Jagan is in slot 2, but not both.
  • Either the singer accompanied by the sarod is in slot 3 or Harpreet is in slot 6, but not both.
  • The Tamil singer is immediately before the singer accompanied by the sarod.
  • Harpreet is immediately before Gulzar.
  • The Marathi singer and the Telugu singer are next to each other.
  • The Urdu singer and the singer accompanied by the sarod are next to each other.
  • There are exactly 2 people between the singer accompanied by the santoor and Jagan.
  • The singer accompanied by the mridangam is somewhere before Jagan.
  • There is exactly one person between the singer accompanied by the guitar and the singer accompanied by the santoor.
  • The singer accompanied by the harmonium is at one of the two ends.
  • Komal sings in Telugu.
  • The singer accompanied by the sarod is somewhere before Gulzar.

z1-d22.title: Hexagonal table (Hard)
z1-d22.html:
Hexagonal table

Six analysts, Mahesh, Nirmala, Oindrila, Prakash, Rohini and Sameer, sit around a hexagonal table in seats numbered 1 to 6 clockwise, all facing the centre (the person on someone's immediate left is in the next seat clockwise). Each covers a different sector, banking, cement, pharma, steel, telecom and textiles, and each has a different rating, A1, A2, B1, B2, C1 and C2.

The following is known:

  • The textiles analyst sits next to the analyst rated C2.
  • The textiles analyst sits next to the pharma analyst.
  • Either the analyst rated B1 sits in seat 1 or the cement analyst sits in seat 5, but not both.
  • Sameer sits next to the cement analyst.
  • The analyst rated B1 sits next to Sameer.
  • The analyst rated A1 sits to the immediate left of the steel analyst.
  • The analyst rated C1 sits next to the telecom analyst.
  • The steel analyst sits next to the telecom analyst.
  • Either Prakash sits in seat 3 or the pharma analyst sits in seat 3, but not both.
  • The analyst rated C2 sits directly opposite the cement analyst.
  • Nirmala sits directly opposite the analyst rated A1.
  • Mahesh sits second to the left of the banking analyst.
  • Prakash sits to the immediate left of Sameer.
  • Oindrila is rated A2.

z1-d23.title: Three-way floors (Hard)
z1-d23.html:
Three-way floors

Six tenants, Tushar, Uma, Vikram, Wasima, Yogesh and Zara, occupy floors 1 to 6 of a building (floor 1 is the lowest). Each has a different profession, architect, dentist, editor, farmer, jeweller and potter; each has a different favourite fruit, mango, guava, papaya, litchi, plum and fig; and each owns a different pet, dog, cat, parrot, hamster, turtle and rabbit.

The following is known:

  • The person who likes mango lives on some floor below the farmer.
  • The hamster owner is also the dentist.
  • Zara lives on the floor immediately below the rabbit owner.
  • There are exactly 2 floors between the floors of the person who likes papaya and the parrot owner.
  • The editor lives on either the top floor or the bottom floor.
  • Either the person who likes fig lives on floor 4 or the architect lives on floor 5, but not both.
  • The person who likes fig lives on the floor immediately below the farmer.
  • The architect and the hamster owner live on adjacent floors.
  • There are exactly 2 floors between the floors of Zara and Tushar.
  • There are exactly 2 floors between the floors of Yogesh and the person who likes guava.
  • Either Yogesh lives on floor 6 or Uma lives on floor 4, but not both.
  • The jeweller is also the person who likes papaya.
  • There is exactly one floor between the floors of Zara and the dog owner.
  • Zara lives on some floor below Yogesh.
  • Tushar and the person who likes papaya live on adjacent floors.
  • The turtle owner lives on either the top floor or the bottom floor.
  • Vikram lives on either the top floor or the bottom floor.
  • Yogesh likes plum.

z1-d24.title: Interview week (Hard)
z1-d24.html:
Interview week

Six interviews of candidates Aarav, Barkha, Cyrus, Damini, Eshwar and Fatima take place on six consecutive days, Monday to Saturday, one per day. Each candidate applies for a different role, analyst, designer, tester, manager, writer and trainer, and each comes from a different city, Nagpur, Surat, Ranchi, Kochi, Jammu and Patna.

The following is known:

  • The candidate for writer is also the candidate from Kochi.
  • Cyrus is scheduled on either the first or the last day.
  • Aarav is scheduled on either the first or the last day.
  • Aarav applies for trainer.
  • There is exactly one day between the days of the candidate for manager and Fatima.
  • The candidate from Ranchi and the candidate for tester are scheduled on consecutive days.
  • The candidate from Nagpur is scheduled on either the first or the last day.
  • The candidate from Ranchi is scheduled on some day before the candidate from Surat.
  • Damini is scheduled on some day before the candidate for tester.
  • There is exactly one day between the days of the candidate for analyst and Barkha.
  • The candidate for designer is scheduled on the day immediately before the candidate for manager.
  • The candidate for analyst is also the candidate from Jammu.
  • Aarav and the candidate from Kochi are scheduled on consecutive days.
  • Barkha and Damini are scheduled on consecutive days.
  • Either the candidate for tester is scheduled on Thursday or Barkha is scheduled on Monday, but not both.

z1-d25.title: Dinner circle (Hard)
z1-d25.html:
Dinner circle

Six guests, Ganesh, Hansa, Inder, Jharna, Kiran and Lubna, sit around a round dinner table in seats numbered 1 to 6 clockwise, all facing the centre (the person on someone's immediate left is in the next seat clockwise). Each is a different profession, doctor, banker, poet, actor, coach and judge; each wears a different colour, red, blue, gold, grey, mauve and cream; and each brought a different gift, flowers, sweets, a book, a plant, wine glasses and a candle.

The following is known:

  • The doctor sits next to the banker.
  • Either Inder sits in seat 1 or the guest who brought a book sits in seat 5, but not both.
  • The guest in grey sits next to the guest in gold.
  • The guest in cream sits next to the guest who brought a candle.
  • Either the guest who brought a book sits in seat 2 or the doctor sits in seat 2, but not both.
  • Ganesh sits second to the left of the guest in red.
  • The judge sits to the immediate left of Jharna.
  • Jharna wears blue.
  • Either the banker sits in seat 6 or Jharna sits in seat 5, but not both.
  • The guest in grey sits next to the guest who brought a plant.
  • The guest in grey sits directly opposite the guest who brought a candle.
  • Kiran sits directly opposite the guest in grey.
  • The guest who brought a plant sits second to the left of the guest who brought wine glasses.
  • The guest in red sits to the immediate left of the guest in blue.
  • Kiran sits directly opposite Hansa.
  • The guest in grey sits next to Jharna.
  • The guest who brought flowers sits directly opposite the actor.
  • The poet sits second to the left of the guest in blue.

z1-d26.title: Craft fair (Hard)
z1-d26.html:
Craft fair

Six stalls in a row at a fair are numbered 1 to 6 from left to right and are run by Madhav, Nupur, Oshin, Pankaj, Radhika and Shaurya, one each. Each stall sells a different craft, baskets, bangles, carpets, dolls, masks and puppets; each was booked on a different date, 1st, 3rd, 5th, 8th, 13th and 21st; and each stallholder comes from a different district, Kutch, Bastar, Kangra, Madhubani, Nalanda and Sivasagar.

The following is known:

  • There are exactly 3 people between Pankaj and Madhav.
  • The bangles seller is at one of the two ends.
  • Either the stall booked on the 13th is in stall 1 or the carpets seller is in stall 6, but not both.
  • The stall booked on the 1st is somewhere to the left of the bangles seller.
  • The carpets seller is immediately to the left of Shaurya.
  • The stallholder from Bastar is immediately to the left of the stallholder from Kutch.
  • Either Pankaj is in stall 6 or the stallholder from Kangra is in stall 2, but not both.
  • There are exactly 2 people between the stall booked on the 1st and Radhika.
  • The stall booked on the 5th and Madhav are next to each other.
  • The stallholder from Nalanda is somewhere to the left of Madhav.
  • The dolls seller is somewhere to the left of the stall booked on the 3rd.
  • Oshin is at one of the two ends.
  • Shaurya and the masks seller are next to each other.
  • Madhav and the puppets seller are next to each other.
  • There are exactly 3 people between the baskets seller and the stallholder from Sivasagar.
  • The stallholder from Kutch and Pankaj are next to each other.
  • The stallholder from Bastar is immediately to the left of the stall booked on the 21st.
